title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We report a preregistered paired trial (N = 500 paired intents) that measured whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single shared LLM generation per intent, deterministic verification, and at most one automated repair—reduces verifier‑unsafe accepted network changes relative to accepting a shared LLM candidate (LLM‑only baseline) on a standardized synthetic NetOps workload. Following preregistration (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we executed 500 distinct intents stratified across 10 synthetic topology profiles using a single declared generator (gpt-5-mini) under shared_initial_generation semantics and a deterministic network verifier enforcing canonical parsing, required sequencing/workflow rules, availability/group constraints, paired‑field dependencies, and final‑state equality to the task expected_final_state. Observed accepted final changes were baseline 496/500 and guarded (GVR) 500/500 with paired contingency n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Under the preregistered exact conditional two‑sided McNemar test (n = 4, k = 4) the two‑sided p = 0.125; the predeclared exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference is [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked in four episodes (one repair attempt each), producing verifier PASSes; total hosted model calls observed = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair), mean model calls per accepted change = 1.008. Because the preregistered decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar, we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the two inferential perspectives, document verifier scope and known blind spots, clarify provider‑call accounting semantics, present artifact‑grounded repaired‑episode diagnostics, and discuss operational implications and limitations grounded in the archived evidence.

sections.introduction: Automating the translation from operator intent to device configuration can substantially reduce manual effort in network operations but introduces risk: incorrect or ill‑sequenced CLI sequences can violate workflow, dependency, or availability constraints and produce outages. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for intent translation and broader AIOps tasks, yet hallucination and factual errors remain primary reliability concerns. A practical architectural mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) gate: produce an LLM candidate for a canonical CLI sequence, deterministically verify that candidate against explicit workflow, dependency, and availability rules, and—when the verifier flags violations—attempt a bounded automated repair. This study asks whether a compact GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → at most one automated repair) reduces verifier‑unsafe accepted changes relative to accepting the shared LLM candidate (LLM‑only baseline) on a standardized synthetic NetOps workload. We executed the preregistered paired protocol (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) on N = 500 paired intents stratified evenly across 10 synthetic topology profiles, using gpt-5-mini for shared initial generation and a deterministic verifier as the adjudicator. All numerical quantities reported are taken verbatim from the archived execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.related_work: Three strands of prior work frame this experiment. First, surveys and system papers document active interest and early deployments of LLMs for intent translation, AIOps, and multi‑agent NetOps orchestration while repeatedly highlighting hallucination and factual errors as obstacles to production automation; these motivate adding deterministic validation gates into tool‑augmented pipelines [1–5]. Second, methodological proposals for evaluate‑and‑repair architectures recommend standardized validator semantics, paired trial designs with preregistration, and explicit accounting for orchestration costs (model calls, repair attempts); these blueprints informed our design and the paired primary estimator. Third, deterministic network configuration verifiers have matured to check syntax, sequencing/workflow patterns, availability constraints, and paired‑field dependencies at scale; such verifiers detect many common LLM mistakes but differ in vendor and control‑plane fidelity. Our experiment situates itself as a controlled, reproducible evaluation of a compact GVR gate using a deterministic verifier that enforces canonical parsing, required‑sequence checks, group/availability constraints, dependency enforcement, and expected final‑state comparison rather than as a claim about production readiness across vendor environments.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The study was fully preregistered (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29). The primary estimand is the paired per‑intent success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) over 500 distinct intents. The confirmatory test predeclared in the registry is the two‑sided exact conditional McNemar on discordant pairs; a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) was predeclared as an exploratory descriptive estimator.

Sampling, tasks, and model scope: Intents were deterministically sampled and stratified evenly across 10 synthetic topology profiles (50 intents per profile) using frozen generation seeds and a deterministic task generator. The preregistration limited model scope to a single declared generator (gpt-5-mini) and prohibited retrieval‑augmented generation. The execution contract specified shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial model call per intent, shared across conditions), independent condition generation disabled, and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1.

Orchestration semantics and provider accounting: For each intent we produced one shared_initial_generation candidate with the declared model. Under the guarded condition the GVR controller validated the shared candidate with the deterministic verifier and—if validation failed—issued at most one repair prompt to the same model. The baseline accepted the shared initial candidate without repair. Provider accounting recorded model_calls_used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls), stage_counts showing shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 4, and mean hosted model calls per accepted change = 504/500 = 1.008. For repaired pairs the observed model calls per pair = 2 (shared initial + one repair). The preregistered execution contract disallowed retrieval‑augmented generation and limited repair depth to one automated attempt.

Deterministic verifier and scoring: The adjudicating verifier canonicalizes CLI sequences and deterministically checks a rule set designed for the synthetic intent grammar. Validation steps include (i) syntactic parsing and normalization; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change); (iii) availability/group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields failing outcome. Per episode the verifier emits normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, a violation list and codes, and boolean valid. A human‑readable codebook maps violation codes to descriptions. The verifier intentionally omits vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing/convergence modeling, session/execution‑time errors, and hardware resource constraints; therefore verifier PASS is necessary for experimental safety but not sufficient for production safety.

Repair policy and transcripts: When the verifier fails the shared_initial candidate the GVR controller constructs a constrained repair prompt containing the original intent abstraction, the verifier violation codes with short descriptions, and an instruction to produce a corrected canonical CLI sequence. At most one automated repair attempt was permitted per failing episode; the repair candidate was accepted only if the verifier returned valid = true. All repair prompts, repair responses, and verifier traces for repaired episodes are archived and summarized in the Results section.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and primary counts: The run completed every planned episode (completed_episode_count = 1000; completed_pair_count = 500) with no failed episodes. Observed accepted‑change counts were baseline 496/500 (0.992) and guarded 500/500 (1.000). Paired contingency counts were n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked in four episodes and each repair attempt produced a subsequent verifier PASS. Provider accounting: model_calls_used = 504 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair = 4).

Confirmatory inferential outcome: The preregistered confirmatory test conditions on the observed discordant margin and evaluates a two‑sided binomial tail on k = n10 with p = 0.5 (exact conditional McNemar). For n = 4 and k = 4 the one‑sided tail P(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = (1/2)^4 = 1/16; doubling for two‑sided yields p = 0.125. Under the preregistered decision rule this p‑value does not meet the preregistered confirmatory threshold and we therefore do not claim confirmatory statistical significance.

Exploratory descriptive estimate: The predeclared paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference is [0.002, 0.016]. This exploratory interval was obtained by resampling paired outcomes and computing the paired difference distribution; because it does not condition on the observed discordant margin and the number of discordants is small, the interval can exclude zero even when the exact conditional McNemar is non‑significant. We report this interval descriptively as predeclared.

Repaired‑episode diagnostics (artifact‑grounded): The four repaired/discordant pairs corresponded to verifier‑detectable sequencing or group/paired‑field dependency violations. The archived violation summaries for the repaired pairs are:
- pair-000090 — violation: MUST_BE_DOWN_FOR_FIELD — ‘‘VLAN/field changed while interface remained admin up; required 'must be down' sequencing violated.’’ — repair_invoked: yes — model_calls_for_pair: 2 — final_score: PASS.
- pair-000341 — violation: MAKE_BEFORE_BREAK — ‘‘Backup uplink not enabled before primary was shut; violates 'make‑before‑break' availability rule.’’ — repair_invoked: yes — model_calls_for_pair: 2 — final_score: PASS.
- pair-000381 — violation: PAIRED_MTU_CHANGE — ‘‘MTU changed on one side of a paired link without coordinating the paired interface’s MTU change.’’ — repair_invoked: yes — model_calls_for_pair: 2 — final_score: PASS.
- pair-000413 — violation: GROUP_AVAILABILITY_CONSTRAINT — ‘‘Both edge interfaces placed admin down simultaneously, violating minimum_active_in_groups availability constraint.’’ — repair_invoked: yes — model_calls_for_pair: 2 — final_score: PASS.
Representative per‑episode verifier diagnostics, normalized configurations, parsed/required command counts, violation lists, and repair prompt/response transcripts for the repaired episodes are archived in the evidence bundle. The numerical totals and contingency counts above are taken directly from the archived analysis.
sections.discussion:
Reconciling McNemar and bootstrap perspectives: The GVR pipeline intercepted four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted; these four constitute the observed discordants (n = 4, k = 4). The preregistered exact conditional McNemar conditions on the observed discordant margin and computes a two‑sided binomial tail; with n = 4 this yields p = 0.125 and thus does not meet the preregistered confirmatory threshold. The predeclared exploratory bootstrap percentile CI excludes zero ([0.002, 0.016]) because bootstrap resampling of paired outcomes does not condition on margin and can repeatedly sample the same small favorable discordant set. Both perspectives are informative: the exact conditional McNemar enforces the preregistered confirmatory decision rule and is conservative for small discordant counts; the bootstrap interval provides a descriptive estimate of magnitude but has reduced frequentist coverage guarantees when discordant counts are sparse. We adhere to the preregistered McNemar decision rule for the primary claim and present the bootstrap interval as predeclared exploratory evidence.

Verifier scope, blind spots, and operational sufficiency: The deterministic verifier enforces canonical normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency and paired‑field checks, and final‑state equality to the task expected_final_state. These checks are necessary to detect many syntactic and workflow errors within the synthetic intent grammar and were sufficient to flag the four repaired episodes in this run. Critically, the verifier does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing and convergence, session execution errors, or hardware resource limits; therefore a verifier PASS is necessary but not sufficient for production safety. Production automation would require expanded verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators, timing/convergence models) and live telemetry‑driven validation (pre‑ and post‑change) before unsupervised execution.

Operational cost, scaling considerations, and failure modes: Under the bounded repair policy (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) the repair invocation rate was 4/500 (0.8%), yielding modest additional model calls: hosted model call events = 504 (500 shared initial + 4 repairs). This low overhead in the synthetic workload indicates that a compact deterministic verifier can act as a low‑latency gate and remove verifier‑detectable unsafe proposals at modest model‑call cost when baseline failure rates are low. Realized benefits depend on baseline failure rates, verifier runtime at inventory scale, adversarial or broader intent distributions, and the latency tradeoffs of higher‑fidelity verifiers. Observed failure modes in this run were sequencing errors, availability‑constraint violations, and paired‑field dependency omissions; these are the classes of mistakes a lightweight verifier is well suited to detect.

Threats to validity and generality: Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration, frozen seeds, deterministic task generation, and complete execution accounting (complete_pair_count = 500; failed_episode_count = 0). Construct validity is limited by the verifier abstraction level and the synthetic device templates: the verifier enforces workflow and group constraints matching the synthetic intent grammar, but these rules imperfectly model vendor behavior and dynamic control‑plane hazards. External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies; multi‑model replication, vendor‑specific parsing, and live telemetry tests are required to generalize. Conclusion validity was affected by realized margins: the preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08; the observed near‑ceiling baseline (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs and reduced realized power relative to the preregistered assumption. These limitations explain why a modest numerical paired difference appears in the exploratory bootstrap interval but not under the preregistered exact McNemar decision rule.

Practical implications and recommended engineering posture: For organizations adopting LLM‑driven intent translation, a compact deterministic verifier used as an automated gate plus a bounded automated repair loop can intercept many verifier‑detectable unsafe proposals with low model‑call overhead in workloads similar to our synthetic setting. Engineering deployment requires calibrating verifier fidelity, permitted repair depth, model selection, and latency budgets against operational risk tolerances, expected baseline error rates, and adversarial threat models. Importantly, deterministic verification should be combined with vendor‑specific parsing, control‑plane simulation or staged dry‑runs, and telemetry‑based post‑change validation to approach production sufficiency.
sections.conclusion: In a fully preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The observed paired difference = 0.008 has an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016] but the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; thus we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance under the preregistered decision rule. Deterministic verification combined with a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in the studied synthetic setting; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated‑automation comparator which was not executed in this run. Archival artifacts including the preregistration, model configuration, raw results, per‑episode verifier traces, provider accounting, and analysis logs are available in the evidence bundle for independent verification and audit (see the preregistration record).

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an explicit autonomy lock. The generation model used in the archived run was gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in the archived model configuration). Key automated components in the run were a deterministic task generator, a deterministic network verifier, and a GVR controller implementing shared_initial_generation plus at most one automated repair per task. The study was preregistered under study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. Primary high‑level execution quantities reported here are: N = 500 complete pairs; model_calls_used = 504; repair calls = 4; paired counts n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The immutable initial master prompt for this run is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt) and its SHA‑256 is 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The design, preregistration, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and this revision were performed autonomously after the autonomy lock; no human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after that lock. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed in this archived run; therefore the original preregistered multiplicity plan that would have adjusted for two confirmatory tests was not applied.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to the deterministic verifier’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation across two planned tests is not applicable to the present execution.
